newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: NZ "political reality" forces rethink on fisheries.
newsitem.headline: NZ "political reality" forces rethink on fisheries.

text.p: "Political reality" had forced a rethink of whether some Waitangi Fisheries Commission assets should be allocated to non-tribal Urban Maori Authorities, commission chairman Sir Tipene O'Regan said on Monday.
"I have talked to a number of tribes to see what level of tolerance or further tolerance they would be prepared to have of assets to go in that direction," O'Regan told reporters at a briefing.
"There is a potential for that to happen because the politicians have to be dealt with," he said.
"Whether they are right or wrong (to seek assets) is immaterial. They are a political reality," O'Regan said.
But he warned of difficulty establishing the urban authorities' mandate. "There is cautious interest, but with whom do you deal and who is mandated to deal?" he asked.
O'Regan and other commissioners had strongly opposed urban authorities' asset claims.
But Maori MPs elected in the 1996 general election, including Maori Affairs Minister Tau Henare, are sympathetic to the urban authorities' position.
O'Regan said assets should be allocated soon.
"Maori development is hemorrhaging, so a settlement is needed," O'Regan said.

The Fisheries Commission has net assets of $400 million representing fish quota, company shares and cash used to settle historical Maori claims. Since it was established in 1992 it has been involved in a wrangle over how they should be distributed.
Early divisions within the commission centred on whether iwi (tribes) should receive assets in proportion to their traditional coastlines or according to their population.
Southern tribes have relatively small populations but long coastlines.

In April a compromise was reached on a portion of the assets which would allocate inshore fishing assets according to a tribe's coastline and allocate 60 percent of deepwater fisheries according to coastline and 40 percent according to population.
The compromise will be put to a major meeting of tribal representatives in Wellington in July which could set the basis for the distribution of the commission's remaining assets.
But the commission has yet to resolve claims by the urban authorities who say they should receive assets because they represent Maori who have few or no links to a tribe.
Under its statute the commission must settle with iwi, ruling out a direct settlement with the urban authorities unless the law is changed.
